To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we give a new construction method of random-like tournaments based on the digraph spectra and the digraph-version of expander-mixling lemma; and (ii) we give a proof of the NP-completeness of the feedback arc problem for tournaments based on the new construction method of (i).
(1) we give a new construction for tournaments that satisfy the quasi-random property, and (2) we prove that the feedback arc set (FAS) problem for tournaments is NP-hard.
we have given a new construction of explicit random-like tournaments and we have shown that the feedback arc set for tournaments is NP-hard.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how can the theory of random-like digraphs be applied to the theory of tournaments?
the following two problems: 1) What is the structure of a random-like tournament? 2) How to construct an explicit tournament which is random-like?
the following two questions: 1. How can we construct explicit random-like digraphs? 2. How can we use the quasi-randomness property to prove hardness of NP-hardness?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have shown that the NP-hardness result of the feedback arc problem for tournaments is a corollary of a result on the existence of explicit random-like tournaments.
our work is a significant contribution to the theory of random-like tournaments.
the feedback arc set for tournaments is a problem that is hard to solve in polynomial time and that is hard to prove NP-hardness of.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the digraph spectra and the digraph-expander mixing lemma are useful in constructing explicit random-like tournaments.
we provide a new construction of random-like tournaments and a new application of the expander theory to the theory of tournaments.
we provide a general framework to construct tournaments with explicit random-like properties, based on the spectra and the expander mixing lemma.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spectral properties of tournaments, and more generally of digraphs, are much more subtle than the spectral properties of undirected graphs, and the spectral theory of digraphs is still in its infancy.
explicit constructions of random-like objects can be obtained by a simple combination of the following two ingredients: (1) an expander mixing lemma and (2) a spectral property of a graph or digraph.

, in contrast to graphs, for which there are several constructions of explicit quasi-random tournaments, the construction of quasi-random tournaments based on spectra is new and has a different flavor from previous constructions.
